feature_request: The CRM should alert us when our relationship with a country goes cold.

proposed_scope_in.item: Nightly job computes last_engagement_date per Country as the most recent existing Engagement record linked to any Contact, Mission, or Project of that country. This is derived on the fly with no new entity or manual field.

A country is flagged 'cold' when days since last_engagement_date exceeds a single global threshold, default 90 days, set as one system config value and not per country. Countries with no Engagement history are flagged once at go-live with a 'no recorded engagement' label.

On transition to cold, the system creates one in-app notification for the Regional Coordinator(s) already assigned to the country. It includes the last engagement date, the last contact engaged, and a link to the Country record.
Weekly email digest to each Regional Coordinator listing their currently cold countries, with the same fields as the notification. Re-reminder at most every 30 days while a country stays cold.
Alert auto-clears when a new Engagement is logged for the country. No acknowledge, snooze, or dismiss action is required of the coordinator.
Notification and digest visibility inherits the existing Country/Mission access model, so users only see alerts for countries they can already see.

proposed_scope_out: Sentiment, relationship-health, or ML scoring of engagement quality
Per-country, per-region, or per-contact thresholds and any settings someone must maintain per country
Dashboards, 'cold countries' lists or queues, and cross-country ranking views
Snooze, acknowledge, dismiss, approval, or escalation workflows
Automatic ingestion of email, calendar, or phone activity to infer engagement
New entities or tables, and new required fields for Regional Coordinators
Alert delivery to channels outside the CRM (SMS, chat) and to users outside existing access roles
Defining which countries or relationships are strategically priority, or what counts as 'cold' diplomatically. This is a policy decision for humans and not a product-design decision.

assumptions.statement: 'Cold' means no logged Engagement of any type with any contact, mission, or project of the country within a single global threshold of 90 days.
assumptions.rationale: A single time-since-last-engagement rule is a deterministic query over existing Engagement data. It needs no scoring model, no per-country configuration, and no new schema, so a small team can ship and explain it in one release.

assumptions.statement: Engagement records already in the CRM are logged as part of normal work and are complete enough to act as the activity signal; Regional Coordinators will not be asked to enter anything extra.
assumptions.rationale: Deriving the alert from existing data honors the zero-data-entry constraint. Asking coordinators to log 'relationship status' fields would rot quickly and defeat the feature.

assumptions.statement: Each country already has an assigned Regional Coordinator in the existing access model, and alerts go to that person and respect existing Country/Mission permissions.
assumptions.rationale: Reusing existing assignment and permissions avoids building a new RBAC or routing system and bounds who can see alert data to those who can already see the country.

assumptions.statement: In-app notification plus a weekly email digest is sufficient timeliness; real-time alerting is not needed because relationships go cold over weeks, not hours.
assumptions.rationale: A nightly batch job and a weekly digest are cheap to build and test, and they avoid alert fatigue and event-streaming infrastructure.

success_criteria: 100% of countries crossing the 90-day no-engagement threshold generate exactly one in-app notification within 24 hours of crossing, verified by back-testing against historical Engagement data
Alerts auto-clear within 24 hours of a new Engagement being logged for that country
No country receives more than one re-reminder per 30 days while it stays cold
Zero new fields or manual steps are required of Regional Coordinators; the feature runs entirely on existing records
Back-test at launch: no more than 25% of ~100 countries are flagged cold on day one. If the share is higher, the threshold is reviewed before release to prevent alert fatigue.
Weekly digest delivered to 100% of Regional Coordinators who have at least one cold country in their portfolio

challenges.challenge_text: A single global 90-day threshold treats Norway and a country with one biannual ministerial cycle identically. Countries with seasonal or low-frequency diplomatic rhythms (parliamentary recess, elections, summit-driven cadence) will be flagged cold every cycle while being perfectly healthy. Regional Coordinators will quickly learn these are noise and start ignoring the digest, so the one genuinely cold high-priority country gets lost in the same pile. The 25% day-one cap still allows ~25 flagged countries, which is already a fatigue-level volume for a coordinator portfolio of perhaps 10-15 countries. Whether 90 days is the right definition of cold is a policy question, but there must be a bounded engineering mitigation, such as a coordinator-visible reason or an exclusion for countries in an active mission.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: Proposer explicitly scopes out per-country thresholds and defers the definition of cold to humans, but ships a hardcoded global default with no mechanism to avoid flagging countries with active missions or known low-cadence relationships. This leaves a real false-positive risk unaddressed.

challenges.challenge_text: The signal is last logged Engagement, but logging is voluntary and uneven. A coordinator who is in weekly phone contact with a ministry but has not logged it will trigger a false 'cold' alert, while a country where an intern bulk-logged a mass-email Engagement looks warm. Turnover compounds this: when a coordinator leaves or a country is reassigned, the backlog of unlogged contact makes the countries look cold exactly when handover is weakest. Also, 'any Engagement of any type' lets low-value records (automated or mass-distribution mailings, a logged circular) reset the clock, hiding a truly cold relationship. The 'complete enough' assumption is untested; the day-one back-test only measures how many are flagged, not whether those flags are true.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: A2 is stated as an assumption with no validation. The back-test success criterion checks only the volume of flags and not their accuracy, so the risk of false positives and false negatives from poor logging data is unmitigated.

challenges.challenge_text: Assumes every country has a current, correct Regional Coordinator. With turnover across 100 countries, some countries will have no coordinator, a departed one (account deactivated), or a stale assignment. The alert then goes to nobody or to the wrong person, and the country silently stays cold with no fallback; the exact failure the feature exists to prevent. In the other direction, a former coordinator who still holds Country access could keep receiving emails with last-contact names for a country they no longer work on. The proposal has no handling for unassigned or inactive recipients.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: A3 asserts the assignment exists but provides no fallback or detection when it does not, and no check that the recipient is still active and authorized at send time.

challenges.challenge_text: The alert and the weekly email include the name of the last contact engaged. Email digests leave the CRM's access-controlled boundary: they sit in mailboxes, are forwarded, are synced to phones, and persist after a user's CRM access is revoked. 'Inherits Country/Mission access' only holds at render time in-app, not for an email sent at 06:00 that is read later. Contact names tied to a country and a 'relationship cold' label are diplomatically sensitive. Also, Engagements may be restricted by mission or classification, so if last_engagement_date or last contact is derived from a restricted Engagement, the alert can leak the existence and the contact of an engagement the recipient cannot see in the CRM. The nightly job computes across all engagements, so it is unclear whether it runs with the recipient's permissions.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: The proposal treats the email digest as equivalent to in-app visibility. It does not state whether the derived fields are filtered per recipient or whether contact names appear in email bodies, so confidentiality leakage via email and restricted-Engagement derivation is unaddressed.

challenges.challenge_text: The go-live behavior and the transition semantics are ill-defined. Countries with no Engagement history are flagged once at go-live; for a CRM that has not been logging engagement consistently, this can dump a large batch of labeled-cold alerts onto coordinators on day one, and 'flagged once' then never re-evaluates them if they are never engaged. Also, 'cold' is an edge-triggered notification, and the re-reminder is only through the digest every 30 days. A job failure or a skipped nightly run could silently miss the crossing, and there is no detection of job failure. The 'exactly one notification' criterion is untestable without idempotency and missed-run handling.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: The Proposer offers no idempotency, missed-run catch-up, or monitoring for the nightly job, and the day-one handling of countries with no history is internally inconsistent with the 'no more than 25% flagged' criterion.

challenge_responses.response: The Critic is right that active-mission countries should not be flagged. The fix is cheap, a rule over the existing Mission entity, so I am adopting it: the cold flag is suppressed while the country has an active Mission, and the notification carries a plain reason line (days since last engagement, threshold in force). I am DEFENDING the single global threshold. Per-country thresholds or seasonality calendars are a setting someone must maintain per country, which is expensive. The residual false positives are bounded: the global value is one config and the day-one back-test is capped at 25%. Whether 90 days is the right definition of cold is diplomatic policy and is routed to humans. Evidence that would justify per-country cadence later: coordinators reporting repeated false cold flags for the same countries after launch.

Logging gaps are real, but the fix options are expensive. Weighting or filtering by Engagement type means a maintained type list, and validating completeness means a review step. Both break the zero-data-entry constraint. Residual risk is bounded in four ways: (1) a false cold alert costs one click to inspect and clears itself the moment the coordinator logs the contact, which is the behaviour we want; (2) the alert shows days-since and links to Country history, so a mass mailing is visible to the coordinator; (3) at handover the alert acts as a prompt to the new coordinator, not a failure; (4) I am adding a release gate where coordinators confirm a sample of 10 flagged countries is truly cold, so accuracy is measured before launch and not just volume. The back-test criterion in the first round measured only volume, and the gate now covers that gap. Evidence that would justify type filtering later: post-launch coordinator feedback showing mass or automated Engagements masking cold countries.

Adopting a cheap, deterministic fix: recipients are resolved at send time from existing data, as the assigned coordinator who is active and still holds Country access. If no one qualifies, the alert routes to existing Operations-role holders with access to that country. This closes both the silent-nobody case and the departed-coordinator-still-gets-emails case with no new table, screen, or settings. The success criteria now test that 100% of cold countries resolve to at least one active recipient. Which role is the right fallback is an organisational and access-authority decision. I am flagging it for a human to confirm and have not invented a policy.

Taking the cheap fix: the weekly email contains no contact names and no engagement dates, only country name, a days-since band, and a link into the CRM. In-app notifications store no engagement details. Last engagement date and contact render at view time through the existing permissions, which removes the email leakage and closes the render-time versus read-time gap. Restricted Engagements count toward 'warm' for the system-run job, so they can only suppress an alert and cannot leak the existence or contact of a restricted engagement. I am DEFENDING against per-recipient recomputation because it is expensive and unnecessary once no engagement details leave the CRM. The only remaining email content is the country name plus a 'cold' label. Whether that label is acceptable in email is a data-classification decision for humans, and I have not set that policy. If humans disallow it, the digest becomes link-only with no country names.

Moving from edge-triggered to level-triggered with one auto-filled column, Country.last_alerted_at on Country. Each night, a cold country with no alert in the last 30 days gets an alert. This makes the job idempotent, lets a skipped run self-heal on the next night, and ensures no-history countries are re-evaluated every 30 days and not flagged only once. No-history countries now count inside the 25% day-one cap, so the earlier inconsistency is resolved. Job failures go to existing platform logging and alerting, with no new screen. Success criteria now include a double-run test and a skipped-run recovery test. A larger monitoring system is out of scope.

challenges.challenge_text: Single global 90-day threshold flags countries with seasonal or low-frequency rhythms and creates alert fatigue for coordinators.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: The Proposer adopted the bounded mitigations I asked for: suppression while a country has an active Mission, a plain reason line showing days-since and threshold, and a day-one 25% cap with a coordinator sample check. The remaining per-country false positives are an acceptable MVP risk. Whether 90 days defines cold is flagged as a human policy decision, and post-launch feedback is named as the trigger for revisiting it.

challenges.challenge_text: Unlogged contact makes countries look falsely cold. Low-value or mass-distribution Engagements reset the clock and hide a genuinely cold relationship, for example an intern bulk-logging a circular for a country with no real contact for six months.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: The defense covers false positives well. A false cold alert is cheap to check, clears itself when the contact is logged, and acts as a handover prompt. The new release gate samples 10 flagged countries. It does not address false negatives. A mass mailing that resets the clock produces no alert, so no coordinator ever looks at the country history the Proposer relies on. The gate only measures precision on flagged countries and says nothing about cold countries that were missed. A cheap fix exists with no new data entry: extend the release gate to also have coordinators review a sample of about 10 unflagged countries whose most recent Engagement is a bulk or multi-recipient record, and record the result. The Proposer should state what happens if that sample shows masking, for example the threshold or type filtering goes back to humans before release.

challenges.challenge_text: Unassigned, departed, or stale coordinator assignments send the alert to nobody or to a former coordinator, so the country stays cold with no one aware.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: Recipients are now resolved at send time and restricted to active accounts that still hold Country access. A fallback to Operations-role holders with access covers the nobody case. A criterion tests that 100% of cold countries resolve to at least one recipient. No new table or screen is needed. Choosing the fallback role is flagged for human confirmation, and that is acceptable for an MVP.

challenges.challenge_text: Email digests leave the access-controlled boundary. Restricted Engagements could leak their existence or date to recipients who cannot see them.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: Most of the engineering risk is closed. The email carries only country name, a days-since band, and a link. Contact names and engagement dates are removed, and a test on rendered output is added. Two points remain that engineers cannot settle. First, whether a country name with a 'cold' label may appear in email is a data-classification decision. Second, the system job counts restricted Engagements toward the clock, so a days-since count can implicitly reflect the recency of an Engagement the recipient cannot see. Whether that is acceptable depends on classification and clearance authority. The Proposer has already stated the link-only fallback if humans disallow the label.

This is sufficient for an MVP.

assumptions.rationale: A single time-since-last-engagement rule is a deterministic query over existing Engagement data. It needs no scoring model, no per-country configuration, and no new schema, so a small team can ship and explain it in one release.

assumptions.statement: Engagement records already in the CRM are logged as part of normal work and are complete enough to act as the activity signal; Regional Coordinators will not be asked to enter anything extra.
assumptions.rationale: Deriving the alert from existing data honors the zero-data-entry constraint. Asking coordinators to log 'relationship status' fields would rot quickly and defeat the feature.

assumptions.statement: Each country already has an assigned Regional Coordinator in the existing access model, and alerts go to that person and respect existing Country/Mission permissions.
assumptions.rationale: Reusing existing assignment and permissions avoids building a new RBAC or routing system and bounds who can see alert data to those who can already see the country.

assumptions.statement: In-app notification plus a weekly email digest is sufficient timeliness; real-time alerting is not needed because relationships go cold over weeks, not hours.
assumptions.rationale: A nightly batch job and a weekly digest are cheap to build and test, and they avoid alert fatigue and event-streaming infrastructure.

success_criteria: Every non-suppressed country over the 90-day threshold gets exactly one in-app notification per 30-day window. Verified by back-test and by rerunning the nightly job twice on the same day (idempotent, zero duplicates).
After a simulated skipped nightly run, the next run produces all missed notifications with no manual intervention.
Alerts auto-clear within 24 hours of a new Engagement being logged for that country.
Countries with an active Mission produce zero cold alerts.
Zero new fields or manual steps are required of Regional Coordinators. The only new schema is the auto-filled Country.last_alerted_at column.
Weekly digest emails contain zero contact names and zero engagement dates (automated test on rendered output).
Delivery test: 100% of cold countries resolve to at least one active recipient with Country access. Countries with no assigned active coordinator resolve to the fallback role.
Day-one back-test: no more than 25% of ~100 countries are flagged, including no-history countries. If the share is higher, the threshold is escalated to humans before release.
Release gate, precision: coordinators confirm a sample of 10 flagged countries as truly cold, and the result is recorded.

Release gate, false negatives: coordinators review a sample of about 10 unflagged countries whose most recent Engagement is a bulk or multi-recipient record, and the result is recorded. If 3 or more of the 10 are judged genuinely cold (the 3-of-10 cutoff is a proposed default for humans to confirm), release is held and the threshold and Engagement-type question goes back to humans before launch.
Weekly digest is delivered to 100% of recipients who have at least one cold country.

challenge_responses.response: The Critic's new point stands: the Round 2 gate measured only precision on flagged countries. A bulk mailing that resets the clock produces no alert, so nobody would ever look at that country's history. The fix is cheap. It is a one-off query over existing Engagement data plus a sample review of about 10 unflagged countries, recorded as a release gate. It adds no screen, table, field, or ongoing review step, and it asks nothing new of coordinators beyond a one-time check, so I am adopting it. I also state the consequence the Critic asked for. If 3 or more of the 10 are genuinely cold, release is held and the threshold and Engagement-type question goes back to humans before launch. The 3-of-10 cutoff is a proposed default for humans to confirm. I am still DEFENDING against in-product type filtering or bulk-mail weighting. That needs a maintained type list and a definition of 'low-value', which is expensive and partly a policy call. The gate measures how large the masking risk actually is, and post-launch coordinator feedback showing masked cold countries would justify adding filtering in a later release.

challenges.challenge_text: Single global 90-day threshold could flag countries with seasonal or low-frequency rhythms and cause alert fatigue. Previously accepted with mitigations: suppression for active-mission countries, a reason line on each alert, and the 25% day-one cap.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: Already accepted. The A1 text is unchanged, so there is no reopen. Status is carried forward.

challenges.challenge_text: Logging is uneven. Unlogged phone contact can cause a false cold alert. A bulk or mass-mailing Engagement can reset the clock, so a genuinely cold country produces no alert and nobody ever reviews its history. The gap left open in Round 2 was that the gate measured only precision on flagged countries.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: The Proposer adopted a one-off false-negative release gate: a query over existing Engagement data for unflagged countries whose latest Engagement is bulk or multi-recipient, plus a recorded review of about 10 of them. It also attached a consequence. If 3 or more of the 10 are genuinely cold, release is held and the threshold and Engagement-type question goes to humans. It adds no new schema, no screen and no coordinator burden. Rejecting in-product type filtering is reasonable for an MVP, because it needs a maintained type list and a 'low-value' definition that is partly a policy call. The 3-of-10 cutoff is explicitly flagged for human confirmation. A sample of 10 is small, but it is enough to detect gross masking before launch. The residual risk of unlogged contact is bounded by the precision gate and the reason line in the alert. Acceptable for an MVP.

challenges.challenge_text: Countries with no coordinator, or with a departed or stale one, could leave the alert going to nobody or to the wrong person. Previously accepted: recipients are resolved at send time, restricted to active accounts that still hold Country access, with an Operations-role fallback.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: Already accepted. The A3 text is unchanged, so there is no reopen. Status is carried forward.

challenges.challenge_text: Email digests leave the CRM's access boundary. Restricted Engagements could leak the existence of an engagement through the alert. Whether restricted Engagements may count toward 'warm', and what the digest may contain, depends on classification and data-sharing policy.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: Already escalated to humans. This turns on classification and policy authority, not engineering. The Proposer's mitigations (no contact names or dates in notifications or the digest, and only a suppression effect from restricted Engagements) are noted. Status is carried forward.

challenges.challenge_text: Go-live behavior for no-history countries, edge-triggered misses on skipped runs, and the lack of job-failure detection. Previously accepted: level-triggered design, an idempotent last_alerted_at column, self-healing reruns, job failures routed to existing platform alerting, and a day-one cap.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: Already accepted. The A1 text is unchanged, so there is no reopen. Status is carried forward.

C1.challenge_text: A single global 90-day threshold treats Norway and a country with one biannual ministerial cycle identically. Countries with seasonal or low-frequency diplomatic rhythms (parliamentary recess, elections, summit-driven cadence) will be flagged cold every cycle while being perfectly healthy. Regional Coordinators will quickly learn these are noise and start ignoring the digest, so the one genuinely cold high-priority country gets lost in the same pile. The 25% day-one cap still allows ~25 flagged countries, which is already a fatigue-level volume for a coordinator portfolio of perhaps 10-15 countries. Whether 90 days is the right definition of cold is a policy question, but there must be a bounded engineering mitigation, such as a coordinator-visible reason or an exclusion for countries in an active mission.
C1.accepted_assumption_text: 'cold' means no logged engagement of any type with any contact, mission, or project of the country within a single global threshold of 90 days

C2.challenge_text: The signal is last logged Engagement, but logging is voluntary and uneven. A coordinator who is in weekly phone contact with a ministry but has not logged it will trigger a false 'cold' alert, while a country where an intern bulk-logged a mass-email Engagement looks warm. Turnover compounds this: when a coordinator leaves or a country is reassigned, the backlog of unlogged contact makes the countries look cold exactly when handover is weakest. Also, 'any Engagement of any type' lets low-value records (automated or mass-distribution mailings, a logged circular) reset the clock, hiding a truly cold relationship. The 'complete enough' assumption is untested; the day-one back-test only measures how many are flagged, not whether those flags are true.
C2.accepted_assumption_text: engagement records already in the crm are logged as part of normal work and are complete enough to act as the activity signal; regional coordinators will not be asked to enter anything extra

C3.challenge_text: Assumes every country has a current, correct Regional Coordinator. With turnover across 100 countries, some countries will have no coordinator, a departed one (account deactivated), or a stale assignment. The alert then goes to nobody or to the wrong person, and the country silently stays cold with no fallback; the exact failure the feature exists to prevent. In the other direction, a former coordinator who still holds Country access could keep receiving emails with last-contact names for a country they no longer work on. The proposal has no handling for unassigned or inactive recipients.
C3.accepted_assumption_text: each country already has an assigned regional coordinator in the existing access model, and alerts go to that person and respect existing country/mission permissions

C4.challenge_text: The alert and the weekly email include the name of the last contact engaged. Email digests leave the CRM's access-controlled boundary: they sit in mailboxes, are forwarded, are synced to phones, and persist after a user's CRM access is revoked. 'Inherits Country/Mission access' only holds at render time in-app, not for an email sent at 06:00 that is read later. Contact names tied to a country and a 'relationship cold' label are diplomatically sensitive. Also, Engagements may be restricted by mission or classification, so if last_engagement_date or last contact is derived from a restricted Engagement, the alert can leak the existence and the contact of an engagement the recipient cannot see in the CRM. The nightly job computes across all engagements, so it is unclear whether it runs with the recipient's permissions.

C5.challenge_text: The go-live behavior and the transition semantics are ill-defined. Countries with no Engagement history are flagged once at go-live; for a CRM that has not been logging engagement consistently, this can dump a large batch of labeled-cold alerts onto coordinators on day one, and 'flagged once' then never re-evaluates them if they are never engaged. Also, 'cold' is an edge-triggered notification, and the re-reminder is only through the digest every 30 days. A job failure or a skipped nightly run could silently miss the crossing, and there is no detection of job failure. The 'exactly one notification' criterion is untestable without idempotency and missed-run handling.
C5.accepted_assumption_text: 'cold' means no logged engagement of any type with any contact, mission, or project of the country within a single global threshold of 90 days

final_decision.feature_request: The CRM should alert us when our relationship with a country goes cold.
final_decision.executive_summary: V1 runs a nightly job that marks a country cold when no Engagement has been logged for more than 90 days (one global threshold) and the country has no active Mission. Each cold country gets one in-app notification per 30-day window. The job is idempotent and self-heals after a skipped night, and alerts auto-clear within 24 hours of a new Engagement. Coordinators enter nothing. The main trade-off was simplicity against accuracy: the Critic pressed on false positives from a single threshold and uneven logging, and on false negatives from bulk-logged Engagements. These were bounded by active-mission suppression, a reason line, a day-one cap of 25%, and a one-off two-part release gate, instead of per-country settings or Engagement-type filtering. The agents agreed on the engineering scope but could not settle the sensitivity of alert content. Three scope items are pending a human decision on C4: the in-app notification content, the weekly email digest, and send-time recipient resolution with its fallback role. Humans must decide whether a country name with a 'cold' label may appear in email and whether restricted Engagements may count toward the days-since figure. They must also confirm the 3-of-10 release-hold cutoff.
agreed_scope_included: Nightly job computes last_engagement_date per Country as the most recent existing Engagement linked to any Contact, Mission, or Project of that country. The job runs with system permissions and counts restricted Engagements toward 'warm', because they can only suppress an alert and never reveal anything. It is derived on the fly with no new entity or manual field.

A country is cold when days since last_engagement_date exceed one global threshold (default 90 days, one system config value, no per-country settings) AND the country has no active Mission. Active-mission countries are suppressed. Countries with no Engagement history are treated as cold with a 'no recorded engagement' label and counted in the day-one cap.

Level-triggered state instead of edge-triggered: one auto-filled column, Country.last_alerted_at, written by the job. Each night a cold country with no alert in the last 30 days gets one in-app notification. Reruns are idempotent and a skipped night self-heals on the next run. Nothing is entered by coordinators.
Alert auto-clears within 24 hours of a new Engagement being logged for the country. No acknowledge, snooze, or dismiss action is required of the coordinator.
Nightly job failures are written to the existing platform job logging and alerting for engineering. No new screen or queue is added.

One-off pre-release release gate, not a product feature: a single query over existing Engagement data lists unflagged countries whose most recent Engagement is a bulk or multi-recipient record. Coordinators review a sample of about 10 of them and the result is recorded. No new screen, table, field, or ongoing review step is added.

scope_pending_human_decision.item: In-app notification carries only the country link, the days-since count, and a reason line ('No logged engagement for N days; threshold 90; no active mission'). Last engagement date and last contact are not stored in the notification. They are rendered on the Country page at view time through the existing Country/Mission/Engagement permissions.

Weekly email digest to each recipient lists currently cold countries with country name, days-since band, and a link into the CRM. It contains no contact names, no engagement dates, and no engagement details.

Recipient resolution happens at send time. Recipients are the currently assigned Regional Coordinators whose accounts are active and who still hold Country access. If none qualify, the alert goes to existing Operations-role holders with access to that country, so the country never goes silently unalerted. Which role is the right fallback is an organisational decision for humans.

agreed_scope_excluded: Sentiment, relationship-health, or ML scoring of engagement quality
Per-country, per-region, or per-contact thresholds, seasonality calendars, exclusion lists, and any settings someone must maintain per country
Weighting or filtering Engagements by type in the running product, for example mass-mailing detection. This is revisited only if the release-gate or post-launch evidence shows masking.
Dashboards, 'cold countries' lists or queues, job-health screens, and cross-country ranking views
Snooze, acknowledge, dismiss, approval, or escalation workflows
Automatic ingestion of email, calendar, or phone activity to infer engagement
New entities or tables, and new required fields for Regional Coordinators
Alert delivery to channels outside the CRM other than the weekly digest (no SMS or chat), and to users outside existing access roles
Per-recipient recomputation of last-engagement values based on each recipient's Engagement visibility

open_questions_for_humans.decision_owner: Head of Diplomatic Security (data classification and clearance authority), with Legal; the product owner should route this
open_questions_for_humans.question: Engineering cannot settle the policy on what an alert may reveal. The Proposer removed contact names and engagement dates from the email and kept only country name, a days-since band, and a CRM link. Two points remain. (1) May a country name with a 'cold' label appear in an email that leaves the CRM's access-controlled boundary? If not, the digest becomes link-only with no country names. (2) May restricted Engagements count toward 'warm' in the system-run job, even though the days-since figure can then reflect an Engagement the recipient cannot see? Please also confirm that the fallback recipient role, currently Operations-role holders with country access, is the right one.
